title: CQRS
subtitle: Command Query Responsibility Segregation: decoupling normalized writes from denormalized read models.
keyTakeaways: Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS) splits an application's data architecture into two models: a Command model for writes, and a Query model for reads.
The Write (Command) model focuses on business invariants and transactional consistency; the Read (Query) model is denormalized and optimized for fast single-table queries.
CQRS introduces eventual consistency between the write database and read projections, requiring strategies to handle the Read-Your-Own-Writes consistency gap.

sections.heading: Separating Write Invariants from Read Projections
sections.body: In standard CRUD architectures, the same database schema serves both writes and reads. As applications scale, this creates conflicting pressures: write operations require normalized 3NF schemas to enforce transactional invariants without anomalies, while complex user interfaces require denormalized views joining data across dozens of tables. CQRS decouples these concerns into distinct models.
bullets: Command Side: Processes mutations (`CreateOrder`, `CancelSubscription`). Operates on a highly normalized relational database or event store; focuses on business validation, locking, and atomic commits.
Query Side: Serves reads. Uses read-optimized data stores (Elasticsearch for full-text search, Redis for leaderboards, denormalized PostgreSQL tables for dashboards). Contains zero business logic.
Asynchronous Projections: Event consumers listen to domain events emitted by the write side (via Kafka or CDC) and project updates into the read databases asynchronously.

sections.heading: Solving the Read-Your-Own-Writes Consistency Gap
sections.body: Because projections update asynchronously, there is a replication lag window (typically 20-200ms) between a command committing and the query database reflecting the change. If a user clicks 'Submit Order' and is immediately redirected to their order history, the query database might return an empty list.
bullets: Return Mutation State Directly: The command endpoint returns the newly created entity payload directly in the HTTP 201 response, allowing frontend single-page apps to update their local UI state without making an immediate query call.
Version / LSN Pinning: The command returns a version watermark; if the client queries before the read store reaches that watermark, route the read temporarily to the primary write database.

tradeOffs.pros: Independent horizontal scaling of reads and writes; read queries are fast single-table index seeks; polyglot storage flexibility.
tradeOffs.cons: Eventual consistency between writes and reads; high operational complexity (managing event pipelines and projections).
tradeOffs.bestFor: Complex domains with massive read-to-write disparities (e-commerce, real-time analytics, booking systems).

tradeOffs.pros: Immediate read-your-writes consistency; single database to operate; straightforward mental model.
tradeOffs.cons: Complex multi-table JOINs degrade read performance; high read volume competes for database locks and IOPS.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Standard CRUD applications and internal business administrative tools.

interviewTip: Address eventual consistency when proposing CQRS: 'We use CQRS to separate our normalized PostgreSQL write database from an Elasticsearch read model. To prevent user confusion from asynchronous projection lag, the command endpoint returns the created entity directly in the response so the frontend updates immediately without waiting for the projection to sync.'
